doc.title: Nancy Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Columbus scene, meeting Cannonball and John Levy
summary: She lists the R&B singers she heard growing up and the Columbus clubs, then recounts meeting Cannonball on a New York corner and John Levy's background with Shearing.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was being in that area of the country, was the music different from when you moved to New York? Did you notice a —

No. No I think we were all pretty much on a — at that time — we’re talking about time that made the difference, as opposed to where you were. Maybe if you were in, if I’d have been in Kansas City I might have sung more blues or R&B. But what I heard as a child, was Little Jimmy Scott, Nat Cole, Bull Moose Jackson, Laverne Baker, Ruth Brown, Dinah. Basically male influences first. Louis Jordan and the Tympani Five. My father was the one who bought records. Consequently what I heard were male influences. I found Dinah and Little Esther, her first record with Johnny Otis, was what was being played at the juke joint around the corner on Kerdosier’s Place. Little Miss Cornshucks. I found I was fifteen before I really heard Ella and Sarah, and it was very much later that I heard Billie. So I came out of more R&B than I did, and blues, than I did jazz. But everybody in Columbus played all of that. We didn’t make those distinctions. There was no such thing as Bobby Short and his jazz trio. It was Bobby Short’s trio. Rusty Bryant’s band. And nobody tagged us. We played – Rusty had hits basically in R&B, but we played, had one of the most brilliant keyboard players Hank Marr, who is now the head of the music department at Ohio State. He’s unbelievable. We had some of the most magnificent people involved with the music in Columbus in small clubs like the Club Regal, the Litchford Hotel, there was a little lounge in there where I played. Rusty Bryant and our band started that whole midwest influx where Miles, Cannon, Bill Evans came with Miles, Bill Doggett, at a place called Marty’s 502, where we stayed for a long time and the next thing, I mean things got so good that all the major jazz artists came through there. And that’s, I met Cannonball though, with Rusty Bryant, in New York City, on the corner standing at 52nd and Broadway. That’s where we met. Cannonball had just come up. He was with John Levy. John Levy, I knew the name. If you were in this business, you knew who John Levy was. John Levy was the former bass player with George Shearing, who became George’s road manager, eventually his manager, and because he © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

did such a good job for George, that just opened the door. By the time I went with John, he had Ramsey Lewis, Gene Harris, The Three Sounds, he had Cannonball, I mean he had so many wonderful artists that he nurtured and made sure that they took care of the business and did wonderful things for them. So the object of my strategy was, if I’m going to do this, the only person who I would trust to help and be there for me would be John Levy.
